title: Sapiens
author: Yuval Noah Harari

parts.title: One human species among several
text: Yuval Noah Harari, a historian at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, tells the whole human story in one book, organised around revolutions. The Cognitive Revolution, about 70,000 years ago, gave our species its peculiar mind. The Agricultural Revolution, about 12,000 years ago, tied it to fields and villages. The Scientific Revolution, which began about 500 years ago, may end it, by giving it the power to remake itself.

He starts by taking us down a peg. Humans first evolved in East Africa about 2.5 million years ago, and for most of that time they were unremarkable animals somewhere in the middle of the food chain. They spread out of Africa across Europe and Asia, and in different places evolved into different species. A hundred thousand years ago the earth was home to at least six kinds of human: Neanderthals in Europe and western Asia, Homo erectus in eastern Asia, the small people of the island of Flores, and others. We are used to being the only humans, and Harari treats that as the strange part.

Our ancestors had paid for their large brains. In Homo sapiens the brain is about 2 to 3 per cent of body weight and uses about a quarter of the body's energy at rest. Walking upright freed the hands but narrowed the hips, so babies are born early and helpless and need years of care, which made humans intensely social. Fire, used daily by about 300,000 years ago, let them cook, and cooking let them digest more food with smaller guts.

Sapiens itself evolved in East Africa, and around 70,000 years ago it began spreading across the world. The other humans then vanished. Harari weighs two theories: that Sapiens interbred with the others, or replaced them. The genetic evidence points to some of each. About 1 to 4 per cent of the DNA that sets modern people of the Middle East and Europe apart is Neanderthal. But the other species did disappear, and Harari suspects Sapiens had a hand in it.

parts.title: Stories that let strangers cooperate
text: What made Sapiens different? Harari's answer is language, and one feature of it in particular. Many animals can warn of a lion. Sapiens could also talk about each other, and gossip let groups keep track of who was trustworthy. But the truly unusual thing was the ability to talk about things that do not exist at all: spirits, gods, nations, laws. You could never persuade a monkey to give you a banana by promising it unlimited bananas after death, in monkey heaven.

Fiction matters because it lets large numbers of strangers cooperate. Chimpanzees live in troops of a few dozen. Human groups held together by personal acquaintance top out at about 150 people, the most anyone can know well. Beyond that, cooperation rests on shared myths. Two Catholics who have never met can work together on a crusade or a hospital, because both believe in the same God. Two lawyers who have never met can defend a stranger, because both believe in laws and human rights.

Harari's example is Peugeot, the car company, named after the family that founded it. You cannot point to Peugeot in its cars or its factories. If every employee died and every factory burned, the company could borrow money and rebuild. If a judge ordered it dissolved, the factories would still stand, but Peugeot would be gone. It exists because lawyers performed the right rituals and enough people believe in it, a kind of legal fiction called a limited liability company.

Harari calls these shared fictions imagined realities, and he insists they are real in their effects. They also gave Sapiens a way to change its behaviour quickly. Other social animals mostly behave as their genes dictate, and change only as their genes change. Sapiens could change by changing its stories: the French went almost overnight, in 1789, from believing in the divine right of kings to believing in the sovereignty of the people.

parts.title: Foragers, and the animals they wiped out
text: For most of their history Sapiens lived as foragers, and Harari argues that our minds are still shaped by that life. Our craving for sweet, fatty food made sense to a forager who found a tree heavy with ripe figs and ate as many as possible before the baboons arrived. In a world of supermarkets the same urge makes us fat.

He paints forager life as better than we usually imagine. Foragers ate dozens of different foods, which protected them from famine when one failed. They had fewer infectious diseases, because most of those come from domesticated animals and crowded settlements. Many worked fewer hours than farmers would. Their lives had real dangers, including high child mortality and violence, and Harari does not pretend otherwise. But the average forager probably knew more about the surrounding world than most of us do.

Foragers were also devastating. Sapiens reached Australia about 45,000 years ago, a journey that meant crossing open sea. Within a few thousand years, 23 of the 24 kinds of Australian animal weighing fifty kilograms or more were extinct, among them giant kangaroos and a marsupial lion. Climate may have played a part, but Harari notes that Australia's animals had survived earlier climate shifts. What was new was us, hunting animals that had not evolved to fear humans, and burning forests to clear them.

The same thing happened in the Americas, which Sapiens reached about 16,000 years ago, and on island after island across the oceans. Mammoths and giant ground sloths disappeared soon after humans arrived, along with many other large animals. Long before anyone wrote a word, Harari concludes, our species had driven to extinction about half of the planet's big land animals. The romantic picture of ancient peoples living in harmony with nature does not survive these numbers.

parts.title: History's biggest fraud
text: Between about 9500 and 8500 BC, in the hill country of the Middle East, Sapiens began to spend nearly all its time tending a few species of plants and animals: wheat, lentils, goats. Within a few thousand years farming had spread across much of the world. The textbook story is that clever humans made their lives easier. Harari calls the Agricultural Revolution history's biggest fraud.

Farmers worked harder than foragers, ate a poorer diet built on one or two crops, and suffered more disease. Their skeletons show slipped discs and arthritis from long days of digging and carrying. A drought or a blight could mean famine. Looking at it from the plant's side, Harari puts it in one of his most quoted lines: "We did not domesticate wheat. It domesticated us." A grass that grew in a small corner of the Middle East now covers vast areas of the planet, tended by humans who clear its fields and carry its water.

Why did anyone accept the deal? Because it came in small steps, each of which seemed sensible. Farming fed more people per acre, so populations grew, and once a village had more children there was no going back to foraging. Each generation had more people living less well. Harari calls this the luxury trap: a gain meant to make life easier becomes a necessity that makes it harder, as email has done for many office workers.

There may have been more to it than food. At Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, people who still foraged built monumental stone pillars around 9500 BC. Harari suggests that such shared projects might have pushed people to settle and grow wheat, rather than the other way round: first the temple, then the village. The domesticated animals paid the heaviest price. In evolutionary terms chickens and cattle are huge successes, but Harari counts them among the most miserable creatures that ever lived.

parts.title: Orders that exist only in our heads
text: Farming produced surpluses, and surpluses fed kings, priests, soldiers and the first cities. Keeping millions of people working together required imagined orders. Harari compares the Code of Hammurabi, written in Babylon around 1776 BC, with the American Declaration of Independence of 1776. The first claims that people are born unequal and sets different penalties according to class. The second claims that all men are created equal. Both, Harari says, are imagined orders. Neither describes anything in our biology, and both work only because people believe them.

Large societies also needed to remember far more than a brain can hold. The Sumerians invented writing, between 3500 and 3000 BC, to keep accounts of taxes and debts. One of the earliest names we can read belongs to an accountant: a clay tablet from the city of Uruk records grain received over thirty-seven months and appears to bear the signature Kushim. Writing began as bookkeeping, and poetry came later.

Then there is money, which Harari calls the most universal system of mutual trust ever invented. The Sumerians paid with fixed measures of barley, and later with the shekel, a set weight of silver. Coins and numbers on a screen work for the same reason barley did: everyone believes everyone else will accept them. Christians and Muslims who could not agree on God happily accepted each other's gold.

Money, empires and universal religions, in Harari's telling, pulled humanity toward a single global order. He is willing to defend empires, the most common form of government for the past 2,500 years. In the second century BC the Romans besieged and destroyed the Spanish town of Numantia. Centuries later, Spaniards celebrated Numantia as a symbol of national courage, in Spanish, a language descended from Latin, as Catholics, under laws based on Roman ones.

parts.title: Admitting ignorance, then conquering
text: The Scientific Revolution, Harari argues, began with a confession. Earlier traditions of knowledge assumed that everything important was already known, by God or by the ancients. Modern science starts from the idea that we do not know, and that what we think we know could be proved wrong. Around 1500, European mapmakers began drawing world maps with empty spaces on them, admitting that there were lands still unknown. That admission sent ships out to fill them.

Science on its own does not explain why Europe came to dominate the world. Harari's answer is that science joined forces with empire and with capitalism. Each fed the others. When James Cook sailed for the Pacific in 1768, his ship carried astronomers to observe the transit of Venus, and botanists and artists to record new plants and peoples. The voyage advanced knowledge, and it also prepared the way for the British occupation of Australia. When Napoleon invaded Egypt in 1798 he took 165 scholars with him.

Capitalism, in turn, rests on a new kind of trust in the future. For most of history the economy hardly grew, so lending was risky and credit scarce. Once people believed the pie would keep growing, they were willing to lend against tomorrow's profits, and the profits paid for more discoveries. Harari's illustration is a fund set up in 1744 by two Scottish ministers, Alexander Webster and Robert Wallace, to support the widows of clergymen. Using the new mathematics of probability, they forecast what the fund would hold in 1765, more than twenty years ahead, and their figure was right almost to the pound.

The darker side of the bargain was force. In 1840 Britain went to war with China to defend the trade of British merchants selling opium there. Belief in growth, Harari observes, did not come with any promise about who would pay for it.

parts.title: Are we any happier
text: After all these revolutions, Harari asks the question historians usually skip: are people happier than they were? Material progress is plain to see. Famine and plague kill far fewer people than they once did, and since 1945 wars between great powers have become rare. Yet happiness depends on expectations, and expectations rise with conditions. Comforts that would have delighted our ancestors become the minimum we expect, so feeling better off is harder than being better off.

Biologists offer another answer: happiness is a matter of chemistry, of serotonin and dopamine, and our brains evolved to give us brief rewards that fade, so that we keep striving. Harari also considers the view that happiness lies in seeing meaning in one's life, whether or not that meaning is a story we tell ourselves. He cites Daniel Kahneman's finding that parents rate the moments of raising children as mostly drudgery, and yet count their children as their greatest source of happiness. And he gives space to the Buddhist position, that suffering comes from craving pleasant feelings, and that the way out is to stop chasing them.

The book ends looking forward. Sapiens is beginning to break the laws of natural selection and replace them with intelligent design. Scientists already engineer bacteria and animals, and are working to connect brains to machines and to extend human life far beyond its natural span. Harari suggests that our descendants may become a different kind of being altogether.

His last pages put the challenge in a question. We have gained the powers of gods, yet we remain unsure of our goals and unaccountable to anyone. Harari's closing warning is that nothing is more dangerous than gods who are dissatisfied and irresponsible and do not know what they want. The question for the future, as he frames it, is less what we can become than what we want to want.

sources: Yuval Noah Harari, Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind (Harper, 2015), ISBN 9780062316097, https://openlibrary.org/isbn/9780062316097
